paras: The Lock Street school race riot was a fight between about 500 white and 150 Black children at the Lock street public school in Cincinnati, Ohio, reported in early October 1903. Some of the Black children were badly beaten and fled to their homes, and the incident reached small-town Michigan papers as a three-sentence wire brief.

According to the brief, "Five hundred white children and 150 colored children" at the school "engaged in a serious race riot." Some of the "colored children" were badly beaten, and they "fled to their homes in terror." The item gives no date for the riot, no cause, and no names of children, teachers, or officials.
No report of arrests, school discipline, or any official response appears in the coverage.

The story ran as one item in a "CONDENSED NEWS" column in the Belding Banner of Belding, Michigan, on October 8, 1903, between notes on a Chicago centennial and a kidnapped boy restored to his mother. The Yale Expositor, also in Michigan, printed the same column with identical wording the next day. Neither paper added comment, and the brief's only characterization was the phrase "serious race riot."
No Cincinnati report and no Black-press account of the riot was found in the coverage.
